hero.title: About <primary>School of Gaming</primary>
hero.subtitle: Where Screen Time Becomes Quality Time. We bring together children, professional Game Educators, and the games children already love — Minecraft, Roblox, Fortnite and more — creating playful learning experiences where they make new friends, develop real skills, and have fun.

quote.text: “What is true now, was once just your imagination.”

mission.heading: Our mission
mission.text: All screen content is not made equal. Gaming is a great hobby when it is treated like all the other hobbies. We use children’s love for games to their advantage — with good friends and a professional Game Educator who is there to guide and help.

playIsEssential.title: Play is essential for children
playIsEssential.description: Play is a child’s work. It is crucial for their wellbeing and development. Our clubs are designed to promote free play that feeds imagination, curiosity, and creativity — powerful tools to face any future.

friendsCarry.title: Friends carry over obstacles
friendsCarry.description: No one should be left without a friend. Moments of play and friendship carry a child over any obstacle in life. In our clubs, children build genuine connections through shared adventures.

keepChildrenSafe.title: Keep children safe online
keepChildrenSafe.description: The Sogverse platform has no direct-message feature: conversation happens in shared group spaces, and chat during a call goes to the whole room and is never stored. Every gamer account is linked to a parent account, and a child signs in through it rather than holding a password of their own. Zero tolerance for bullying and toxicity.

familyInTheLoop.title: Family in the loop
familyInTheLoop.description: Parents are partners. You stay in control of your child’s gaming experience while they enjoy the freedom to explore, create, and make friends in a safe environment.

howClubsWork.heading: How our clubs work
howClubsWork.paragraph1: Each week, our gamers log in and are greeted by their own Game Educator — a Gedu. The Gedu guides them through the day’s topic, giving children space and freedom to make the adventures their own.
howClubsWork.paragraph2: Our Gedus are gamers themselves. They understand firsthand that as children and teenagers, identity and friendships are built both online and offline. That understanding shapes every session they lead.
howClubsWork.paragraph3: All our clubs are built around stories that give space for gamers to explore, create, and imagine. Between weekly sessions, gamers get fun challenges to do online and offline. During holidays we organise camps, and every week there are community events, tournaments, and competitions.
howClubsWork.paragraph4: Every gamer takes an oath to behave kindly and righteously — whether in-game, on voice chat, or in everyday life. The same values apply everywhere.

forParents.heading: For parents
forParents.paragraph1: Parental game education is just as important a part of what we do as the clubs themselves. We want to help parents keep up with the ever-changing gaming world so they can support their children with confidence.
forParents.paragraph2: You stay in control — managing accounts, enrolments, and spending — while your child enjoys a safe environment guided by professionals who care.

whatIsSogverse.question: What is Sogverse?
whatIsSogverse.answer: Sogverse is School of Gaming’s platform for clubs, camps and events in Minecraft, Roblox, Fortnite and more, led by professional Game Educators — Gedus, as everyone here calls them.

isItASchool.question: Is this school?
isItASchool.answer:
No. Gaming is a hobby like any other, and that is how we run it: a Game Educator is there to guide and help, not to grade. Nothing in Sogverse gives a child a mark, sets homework or holds an exam.

What your child does get is a group of their own, a Gedu who knows them, and a written report after each session so you can see what they worked on and how it went.

ages.question: What ages is this for?
ages.answer:
Every club, camp and event carries its own age range, shown on its page and on its card in the shop — and the shop has an age filter to help you find what fits your child. Across the platform those ranges run from age 7 to 17.

The games themselves carry their own age ratings, and every game’s rating is shown on the page of the club, camp or event built around it. We never run a game rated 18+. In Finland we follow the national age-rating guidance, which lets a child play a game rated up to three years above their own age when a parent is present and comfortable with it.

Wherever you are, the game’s rating and the activity’s own age range are both on the page before you sign up, and signing your child up confirms you are happy with them.

games.question: Which games do you run, and does my child need to own the game?
games.answer:
Our clubs, camps and events run in Minecraft (Java, Bedrock and Education editions), Roblox Studio, Fortnite, Rocket League and Pokémon GO, alongside sessions on esports, programming, AI and game creation — every club, camp and event page names the game it is built around and says plainly what you need.

Fortnite, Rocket League, Pokémon GO and Roblox Studio are free to download; your child needs a free account for them.

Minecraft Java and Minecraft Bedrock are paid games your family buys once from the publisher — the price is not included in ours, and the edition matters, so the page tells you which one and where to get it. For Minecraft Education there is nothing to buy and no school account to arrange: School of Gaming provides the accounts used in the session, and your child only downloads the game itself, free of charge.

equipment.question: What equipment does my child need?
equipment.answer:
It depends on the game, and every club, camp and event says so on its own page.

Minecraft Java needs a computer — Windows, Mac or Linux — and the console, phone and tablet edition will not work. Roblox Studio runs on Windows PCs and Macs only: not on a tablet, Chromebook, phone or console. Minecraft Bedrock runs on consoles, phones, tablets and Windows PCs, and Rocket League on Windows PCs, PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo Switch. Pokémon GO needs a phone or tablet with GPS and a mobile data connection, because it is played outdoors.

Online sessions themselves run in the browser, over voice, so your child also needs a microphone — the session screen has a microphone picker and a live test bar so they can check it is the right one before they speak.

productTypes.question: What’s the difference between clubs, camps, and events?
productTypes.answer: Clubs meet on a recurring schedule. Camps run across multiple days during school breaks. Events are one-off get-togethers.

billing.question: What does it cost, and how does billing work?
billing.answer:
Prices are set per club, camp and event, and each one shows its own price on its page, in euros and including VAT.

How you pay depends on what you are signing up for: a club is a monthly subscription, billed every month with no fixed commitment; a camp or an event is a single payment made once at signup, with nothing further to pay; and a municipality club is paid for by the municipality, so there is nothing to pay us. Each child’s place in each club is its own monthly subscription, named after the child and the club, so a family with two children in two clubs sees four lines. If you sign up before a club has started, nothing is charged that day: the page tells you the date of your first payment before you commit.

Your saved cards, invoices and subscriptions all live in the Payment & billing card on My SOG, which opens Stripe’s own secure billing page.

cancellation.question: Can I cancel, and what is your refund policy?
cancellation.answer:
A club runs as a monthly subscription with no fixed commitment, and you can cancel whenever you like, at no cost, from the Payment & billing card on My SOG, which opens Stripe’s secure billing page. Your child keeps their place until the end of the billing period you have already paid for — their club page shows the date of their last session while the membership winds down.

Every club also carries a 30-day money-back guarantee: if it turns out not to be right for your child, email {supportEmail} within 30 days of their first session and we refund everything you have paid towards that club — there is no form and no reason to give.

Camps are booked and paid as a one-off, so they work differently: cancel 14 days or more before the camp starts and you get a full refund; between 7 and 14 days before, we refund you minus a €50 administration fee; less than 7 days before we cannot refund the payment, because the place has been held and prepared for your child — unless it is a medical emergency or something genuinely outside your control. If your child cannot attend because of illness, send us a doctor’s certificate at {supportEmail} and we refund you.

severalChildren.question: I have several children — how do accounts and payments work?
severalChildren.answer:
You hold one parent account, and you create a gamer account for each child from My SOG — first name, birth month and year, and optionally gender. A child never creates an account of their own, and your account can hold up to seven gamers.

Paying is yours to do: each child’s place in each club is its own line, so you can see and cancel them one at a time, and you reach them all from the Payment & billing card on My SOG.

There is no per-family bundle to buy and no separate account to set up per child.

languages.question: What language are sessions run in?
languages.answer:
Two different settings, and they do not have to match.

Every club, camp and event is delivered in one language — Finnish, Swedish, English or French — shown on its page and usable as a filter in the shop.

Separately, the language you read Sogverse in is your own choice, from the picker in the site header. Changing it changes the app, not the language your child’s sessions are run in, so a Finnish-speaking parent can read the site in Finnish and enrol their child in an English club.

municipalityClubs.question: What is a municipality club, and how do we join one?
municipalityClubs.answer:
A municipality club is a club we run together with a Finnish municipality. Depending on the municipality it meets either online from home or in person at your child’s school, and a professional Game Educator is there to guide it either way.

The municipality pays for it, so there is nothing to pay us when you register — some municipalities charge families a small fee of their own, which they will tell you about. You do not need a code or a referral: search for your municipality on our municipality clubs page, and if we have reached it, its clubs are listed there and you register your child directly, with no payment step.

Places are limited and clubs often have a waiting list, so if your child stops attending, please tell us so the place can be offered to the next gamer. We also run clubs that are open to everyone, which a gamer can join wherever they live.

whoLeads.question: Who leads the sessions, and how are Gedus vetted?
whoLeads.answer:
Every session is hosted by a Gedu — a Game Educator who’s also a gamer and knows how to support children in-game and out.

We require every Gedu to show us a criminal record extract for working with children before we certify them — the Finnish rikosrekisteriote, which they order themselves from the Legal Register Centre and which must be less than six months old when they show it to us — and to read and accept the contract they work under. We keep no copy of the extract and record nothing out of it, only that an acceptable one was shown and when.

Registering as a Gedu opens no group on its own: until an admin certifies the account, a Gedu cannot be assigned to a group or use the Gedu tools.

safety.question: Can strangers talk to my child, and is anything recorded?
safety.answer:
No — a club’s voice room is not a public room anyone can find. It exists only during that group’s session window, opening five minutes before the session starts and closing five minutes after it ends, and the only people who can enter are the members of that group, a Game Educator working on that club, and School of Gaming admins; that check runs on our server every time someone joins, so a child with no place in that group has no way in.

There is no direct-message feature anywhere on the platform: a session’s chat goes to the whole room, never to one child privately, and it carries pictures as well as words. It lives in the room, which is open for that same window — that is where your child reads it, and once the room closes there is no way to open it again. We do keep it: the Gedus running that club and School of Gaming admins can look back at what was said, which is what makes moderating it possible. Removing a message leaves a marker in its place rather than erasing it.

The session itself is not recorded. Nothing in the app records, transcribes or stores the voice or video of a session, and the room carries no recording controls.

Only the Gedu and admins hold the moderator controls, and those reach a long way: muting a microphone or locking it, turning a camera off or locking it, muting someone in the chat, moving someone into a space of their own, and speaking to every space at once. In-game chat is a separate thing, run by the games themselves — on School of Gaming’s own Minecraft server our Gedus can mute, kick and ban a player.

gamerAccounts.question: How does my child sign in, and what is the parent PIN?
gamerAccounts.answer:
Your child has no login of their own. A gamer account carries an internal Sogverse address rather than your child’s real email address, it is linked to your parent account, and your child enters Sogverse by switching to their profile from yours — there is no password for them to lose or share.

Getting into the parent side takes a four-digit PIN that only you know, so a password saved in the browser is not enough to buy anything or change a child’s account, and the session locks again the moment you switch to a child’s profile or sign out.

If you forget the PIN, we email a reset link to the address on your account and nowhere else — a child pressing “Forgot your PIN?” simply sends you an email.

childData.question: What do you store about my child?
childData.answer:
About your child:

Their first name, their birth month and year — we do not ask for the day — and optionally their gender.Your family surname, because your child is part of your family. It is shown to nobody outside your family: a Gedu’s roster and the voice room show your child’s first name, their age, and any game username you have added.An internal Sogverse address on their account, rather than a real email address.Optionally, their username in the games their clubs use — today Minecraft and Roblox — and the id that game gives them, so we can recognise them in a session. Their in-game character picture is loaded from that game’s own servers, so the username reaches Minecraft or Roblox whenever a roster is drawn.A profile picture that is not a photo: with no game account linked, the image beside their name is a pattern generated from their account id.

Alongside that we keep what running a club requires: which clubs, camps and events they are signed up for, their attendance, the session reports and short staff notes their Gedus write, the chat from their sessions and any picture posted into it, anything they make that a Gedu links to their group, the consents recorded against their place, and the photos a Gedu attaches to a report. A Gedu’s moderation is on record too — a child moved into a private space, or muted in the chat, leaves a record of it. Those report photos are of the session rather than of one child — every family in that group sees them on the group’s page and receives them with the report by email.

To see, correct or delete anything we hold about your child, email {supportEmail}. We keep your information for as long as you have an account and delete or anonymise it if you close one, except where the law requires us to keep certain records longer, as Finnish accounting law does for payment records.

howToStart.question: How do I get started?
howToStart.answer:
Create a parent account, add your child as a gamer from My SOG, then browse the shop and enrol them — the signup panel asks who the seat is for, and prompts you to add a gamer if you have not yet.

Once you have signed up we place your child in a group with a Gedu before their first session, and the club then appears on My SOG for both of you.

They join sessions through your account — you switch to their profile — so they never need a password of their own.

becomeGedu.question: How do I become a Game Educator?
becomeGedu.answer:
Register for a Gedu account on our Game Educator sign-up page: it asks for your name and email, a password, and optionally your phone number, the languages you speak, the areas you can work in on site, and your Minecraft or Roblox username. You can sign in straight away.

Before an admin certifies your account we ask two things of you: read and accept the contract you would work under, and show us a criminal record extract for working with children (rikosrekisteriote), which you order yourself from the Legal Register Centre and which must be less than six months old — we keep no copy of it.

Certification is what opens the rest: until then you cannot be assigned to a group or use the Gedu tools.

joiningSession.question: How do I join my session when it starts?
joiningSession.answer:
Here is the whole thing:

Open My SOG and find your club.Look at the button on it. Until your session is close it stays locked, and it tells you the day and time it opens.Five minutes before your session starts, that button changes to “Join voice room”.Tap it. You are in.

There is nothing to install and no code to type.

If your club says instead that you are signed up and we are matching you with a Gedu and a group, there is no button on it yet. You are in — we just have not put you in a group. That happens before your first session, and your Gedu will be there when it does.

cannotBeHeard.question: Nobody can hear me — what do I check?
cannotBeHeard.answer:
Check these in order. It is almost always the first one.

Is your microphone button red? That means you are muted. Tap it to unmute.Does the button show a padlock? Your Gedu has locked your microphone for a moment. They will unlock it.Tap the small arrow next to the microphone button. It opens your microphone settings, where you can pick the right microphone from the list.Now talk, and look for the bar under the list. If there is no bar at all, your microphone is off rather than quiet — go back to step 1. If the bar is there but never moves, something else on your device has your microphone.

If you see a red message saying we cannot reach your microphone, close any other app or tab that is using it, allow microphone access in your browser’s settings, and tap Reload.

Still nobody? Tell your Gedu in the session — they can help.

cannotHearOthers.question: I cannot hear anyone — what do I check?
cannotHearOthers.answer:
Check these in order:

Turn your device’s volume up, and check your headphones are plugged in properly.Look at the zones. You only hear the people in the same zone as you, so if everyone else is somewhere else, tap the zone they are in to move in with them.If your Gedu moved you into a zone on purpose, stay there. They will bring you back.

If the others are in your zone, your volume is up and it is still silent, tell your Gedu — say it out loud, or write it in the chat if your room has one. They can see who is in the room and help.

someoneIsMean.question: What if someone is mean to me in a session?
someoneIsMean.answer:
Tell your Gedu or a parent. You never have to deal with mean behaviour on your own, and telling an adult is not telling tales.

Your Gedu will always take it seriously and help sort out what happened. Being mean to others or breaking the club rules has consequences. Everyone has the right to feel safe and welcome in the club.

certification.question: What does certification mean, and what can I not do until then?
certification.answer:
Certification is an admin confirming your account is ready to work with children. Two things come before it: accepting your Gedu contract, and presenting a criminal record extract for working with children (rikosrekisteriote) that is less than six months old. You order the extract yourself from the Legal Register Centre. We keep no copy of it and record nothing out of it — only that an acceptable one was shown, and when. Your contract page shows where both of them stand.

Until you are certified you cannot be assigned to a group, and your Tools section stays closed: you cannot start an instant voice room, and you cannot reset Minecraft Education passwords. You also cannot email a session report to families or add photos to one.

Everything else is open now: signing in, My SOG, your profile and coverage areas, and reading and accepting the contract. Help & feedback is here whether or not you are certified — use the form above if you are waiting and want to know where you stand.

groupAssignment.question: How do I get assigned to a group?
groupAssignment.answer:
An admin assigns you. Assignments are made from a club, camp or event’s groups panel on the admin side — you cannot assign yourself, and there is no request to submit — and you can hold one group per club, camp or event.

Two things decide whether you appear as an option: your account has to be certified, and the admin picking a Gedu sees the languages you speak beside your name and can filter on them, so keeping your spoken languages up to date in your settings is what puts you in front of the right groups. Your coverage areas are for something else — finding you as a substitute when another Gedu cannot cover a session — so they are worth keeping current too.

There is no email when an assignment is made — the group and its next session appear on your My SOG the next time you open it.

takingAttendance.question: How do I take attendance?
takingAttendance.answer:
From your My SOG:

Open the club, camp or event you run. Its sessions are all listed on its page.Find the session and tap Edit.Attendance is the first thing in the editor: one row per gamer, each with Present and Absent.Mark every gamer on the list, then tap Save.

A row starts unmarked, and unmarked is a real third state rather than a quiet “absent”. Tapping an answer you have already chosen clears it again, so a wrong tap costs nothing, and the counter above the list tells you how many of the group you have marked so far.

You can save a half-marked sheet and finish it later — nothing you have already marked is lost. There is deliberately no “mark all present”: the register is also your confirmation that the session ran, and it is what you are paid on. Saving it does not finish the session on its own, though — the report and sending it to the families are the rest.

attendanceAlert.question: Why does my club still show a yellow “needs attention” mark?
attendanceAlert.answer:
Because that session still owes something. When a finished session is flagged, it is one of these four:

Every gamer on the group’s current roster is marked, present or absent.A session report has been written. Text you wrote in the plan beforehand counts as one, so revise it into what actually happened.That report has been sent to the families.On the last session of a run that requires creations, every member has one.

The first is by far the most common reason. Marking the gamers who turned up is only half the register — the ones who did not turn up need marking Absent, or their rows stay unmarked and the session stays flagged.

One other thing reopens a session you had already finished: a gamer who joins the group afterwards. Nobody has said yet whether they were there, so their row comes back unmarked and waits for you.

safeguardingConcern.question: I have a safeguarding concern mid-session — what do I do?
safeguardingConcern.answer:
Deal with the immediate situation in the room first — you hold the moderator controls: mute a microphone, lock it, or move someone into a private space away from the group. Then put it on record the same day, while it is fresh.

Every session has a staff note, marked for Gedus and admins, that families never see; it is where an incident, bullying or a worry about a gamer belongs. There is also a per-gamer note on the group roster that stays with that child in that group, session to session, and is likewise Gedu- and admin-only. Neither is visible to any family.

A note is a record, not an alert: nobody is paged by it, so anything urgent, or anything that needs someone beyond the group, goes to the office at {supportEmail} as well.

gamerCannotConnect.question: A gamer cannot connect and the session has started — what can I do?
gamerCannotConnect.answer:
Two things you can do inside the product, and one you cannot.

Check who is actually in the room against your roster — the participant list only shows people who are connected right now, so a name missing from it is a gamer who has not made it in, and nothing marks that for you; you read it off the list.

To reach the family, open the group’s roster in the group workspace: each row carries the family’s contact email, which you copy with a tap, and there is a copy-all control above the list. You send from your own mail — there is no in-app message to a family, no text message, and no phone number on the roster.

What you cannot do is admit them yourself: entry is decided by our server on the gamer’s own request, and they need an active place in that group with the session window open. If they hold a place and still cannot get in, the fastest fix is usually on their side — allow the browser microphone access, close whatever else is using it, reload. If it is something we need to fix, mail the office at {supportEmail}.

minecraft_java.description: Minecraft is a creative building game — think digital LEGO. Children explore a blocky world, gather materials and build whatever they imagine, from a cosy house to a whole city. There’s no winning or losing; it’s a calm, open-ended space to create and problem-solve. “Java” is the original version for Windows, Mac and Linux computers — the one our remote clubs use, because it supports the tools our Game Educators rely on.
minecraft_java.note: For our clubs your child needs Minecraft on a computer. On Minecraft.net it’s sold as “Minecraft: Java & Bedrock Edition for PC” — a single one-time purchase (not a subscription) that includes the version we use. The separate console, phone and tablet version won’t work for these clubs.

minecraft_bedrock.description: Minecraft is a creative building game — think digital LEGO. Children explore a blocky world, gather materials and build whatever they imagine, from a cosy house to a whole city. There’s no winning or losing; it’s a calm, open-ended space to create and problem-solve. “Bedrock” is the version that runs on consoles (Xbox, PlayStation, Switch), phones, tablets and Windows PCs.
minecraft_bedrock.note: Your child needs Minecraft Bedrock for this club. It isn’t included in the price — buy it from the store that matches the device your child will play on (the same game, sold in a different place on each device). On a games console, playing online may also need that console’s paid online membership.

minecraft_education.description: Minecraft is a creative building game — think digital LEGO. Children explore a blocky world, gather materials and build whatever they imagine. Minecraft Education is a version made for the classroom: the same friendly, open-ended building, plus extra tools for the adult leading the session, designed for guided activities rather than solo play.
minecraft_education.note: There’s nothing to buy and no school account to arrange — School of Gaming provides the Minecraft Education accounts participants use during the club. For our remote clubs, your child also needs to download the game itself, free of charge, from the Microsoft Store or from Minecraft Education’s own site.

fortnite.description: Fortnite is a colourful, cartoon-style online game where players team up and compete in short, round-based matches. It’s hugely popular and very social — children play together with friends. The look is bright and non-realistic (no blood or gore), though matches are competitive and played online with others.
fortnite.note: Fortnite is free to download and play — you don’t buy the game itself. Your child creates a free Epic Games account to play. Some optional extras (outfits and such) cost money, which you can limit with parental controls.

pokemon_go.description: Pokémon GO is played outdoors, on a phone. Creatures appear on a map of the real world, and children walk to parks, streets and landmarks to find and collect them. It’s about collecting rather than fighting — the appeal is exploring, filling up a Pokédex and comparing finds with friends. Most of the playing happens on foot, so it tends to get children moving.
pokemon_go.note: Pokémon GO is free to download and play — you don’t buy the game itself. Your child needs a phone or tablet with GPS and a mobile data connection, plus a free account. There are optional in-app purchases, which you can limit with parental controls. Because it’s played outdoors in real places, it’s worth agreeing in advance where your child may go and whether an adult comes along.

roblox_studio.description: Roblox Studio is the free tool that Roblox games themselves are made with. Children design worlds, build with real 3D tools and script with real code, turning their own ideas into experiences other people can actually play. In our clubs they create rather than play — it’s a first step into real game development.
roblox_studio.note: Roblox Studio is free — there’s nothing to buy. It runs on Windows PCs and Macs only: not on an iPad or other tablet, not on a Chromebook, phone or games console. A free Roblox account is needed too, and the account’s age setting governs its chat and privacy controls. Finished creations can be published for other players to find and play.

rocket_league.description: Rocket League is football played with rocket-powered cars. Two teams drive around an arena and try to push an oversized ball into the other team’s goal, in short matches of about five minutes. The look is bright and cartoonish and there’s no violence — it’s a sport, not a shooter — so it’s easy to follow from the sidelines even if you’ve never played it yourself. Almost every goal comes out of the team working together, which is why it suits club play so well.
rocket_league.note: Rocket League is free to download and play — you don’t buy the game itself. Your child needs a free Epic Games account. It runs on Windows PCs, PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo Switch, and players on different devices can play together, so your child’s device doesn’t have to match anyone else’s. There are optional in-game purchases (decorations for the cars), which you can limit with parental controls.

programme.question: What is the Programme?
programme.answer:
A free game-design programme where young people learn to build on Roblox, run by Lynx Educate and School of Gaming, in collaboration with Roblox.

It runs both online and in person across France, and finishes with your child publishing their own game or item.

eligibility.question: Who can take part?
eligibility.answer: Young people in France aged 13–17, registered by a parent or legal guardian.

cost.question: Does it cost anything?
cost.answer: No, the Programme is 100% free for registered families!

experience.question: Does my child need Roblox experience already?
experience.answer: No prior experience needed — sessions are designed to teach game-building from the basics through to publishing.

where.question: Where do sessions happen?
where.answer:
In-person sessions run in Paris, Lille, Strasbourg and Bordeaux. Online sessions are open to families anywhere in France.

Sessions range from 60 minutes to 9 weeks.
where.answer2: See each specific event for details.

language.question: What language are sessions delivered in?

equipment.question: What equipment does my child need?
equipment.answer: A computer (Windows or Mac) connected to the internet, plus access to Roblox Studio.
equipment.answer2: For online events, gamers should join with their own computer with Roblox Studio installed. For in-person events, computers and equipment will be available at the venue.

dataSharing.question: Is my child’s information shared with Roblox?
dataSharing.answer: Some account information is shared with Lynx Educate and Roblox to deliver the Programme and to evaluate the Programme’s efficacy. Full detail is in our Privacy Policy.

media.question: Will my child be photographed or filmed?
media.answer: Sessions may be photographed for internal records. Whether footage is used externally in marketing is entirely your choice at registration, and you can change it anytime.

intro.heading: The short version — for parents and young people
blocks: The Programme is for young people in France aged 8–17. A parent or legal guardian must complete registration.

We collect only what we need to register your child, deliver the Programme safely and understand whether it is working. This includes the parent’s contact details, limited information about the child, the child’s Roblox username or User ID, and information about attendance, completion and game publication.

School of Gaming uses information to operate the registration and learning platform. Lynx Educate processes Programme information as needed to manage delivery. Each organisation has different responsibilities depending on the activity and the purpose for which personal information is used.
School of Gaming is the data controller for the operation of Sogverse and the personal information it processes for its own platform services.

For the limited Programme impact research carried out on behalf of Roblox, Roblox is the data controller, Lynx Educate acts as Roblox’s data processor, and School of Gaming acts as Lynx Educate’s approved sub-processor.

Where Lynx Educate processes personal information for its own independently determined purposes (such as optional Lynx email communications), Lynx Educate acts as the data controller for that processing.
The following choices are optional and will not affect your child’s place:
Emails to the parent from Lynx Educate about future Roblox events and gaming resources.
Photography or filming for private Programme reporting to Roblox.
Public use of photographs or footage by Lynx Educate, School of Gaming and Roblox.
Routine online sessions are not recorded. A child will not be photographed or filmed where the required permission has not been given or where the child does not want to take part.
Lynx Educate and School of Gaming do not sell Programme registration information or use it to advertise to children.
You and your child may ask to see, correct or delete information, withdraw an optional consent, or object to certain uses by contacting support@lynxeducate.com or {supportEmail}.

We will not deliberately photograph or film a child who objects, even where a parent previously selected a media checkbox. Staff will use reasonable practical measures to keep children without permission out of identifiable footage.

mediaCaseStudies.heading: Case studies, names and participant-created content
blocks: The two registration media boxes cover photographs and footage only.
A separate written release will be obtained before using:
A child’s full name.
A named or detailed case study.
A testimonial or quotation.
An audio interview.
Identifiable survey responses.
Game screenshots linked to the child.
Participant-created content or intellectual property.

mediaChanging.heading: Changing a media choice
blocks: A parent or child may withdraw a media permission by contacting us or using the available Sogverse setting.

After withdrawal, we will stop new uses and remove material from channels we control where reasonably possible. Withdrawal cannot make earlier lawful use unlawful, undo printed materials already distributed, or guarantee deletion of copies already shared by third parties.

childSafety.heading: Children’s privacy and safety
blocks: The Programme uses a private and moderated learning environment.
Every child’s profile is linked to a parent or guardian account.
Children take part under their first name only — never their contact details.
Only registered participants and vetted Game Educators may join.
Communication is group-based and supervised.
There is no private direct messaging between children.
Routine sessions are not recorded.
Lynx Educate and School of Gaming do not use Programme registration data for behavioural advertising to children.

Safeguarding concerns are handled under the joint <linkRobloxSafeguarding>Child Safeguarding Policy</linkRobloxSafeguarding>. School of Gaming handles day-to-day concerns in the first instance and escalates serious matters to Lynx Educate. Emergency services are contacted first where a child may be in immediate danger.

Children must also receive an age-appropriate explanation of how their information is used. French law requires information addressed to a child to be clear and easily understandable. Where an online processing activity genuinely relies on consent and concerns a child under 15, French law requires the child and the holder or holders of parental authority to consent jointly.

helpers.heading: Who else helps us deliver the Programme
blocks: Information may be accessed only where necessary by:
Authorised Lynx Educate personnel.
Authorised School of Gaming personnel and trained Game Educators.
Roblox for the limited research and consented media uses described above.
Event venues, accessibility providers or photographers that need limited information for a particular activity.
Professional advisers, insurers, emergency services, safeguarding bodies or public authorities where required.
Technical providers that operate Sogverse.
School of Gaming’s principal technical providers currently include:
Supabase, for account and Programme information.
Brevo, for operational emails and reminders.
Daily.co, for live voice and video functionality.
Vercel, for website hosting and privacy-friendly analytics.
Meta/WhatsApp, only where a family chooses WhatsApp communications.
These providers may process information only to perform their contracted services and must protect it appropriately.

transfers.heading: International transfers
blocks: Lynx Educate is based in France and School of Gaming is based in Finland.
Roblox is based in the United States, and some technical providers may also process information outside the European Economic Area.

Where information is transferred outside the EEA, the responsible organisation uses an approved transfer mechanism, such as an adequacy decision or the European Commission’s Standard Contractual Clauses, together with appropriate security measures.
The Roblox–Lynx Data Processing Addendum includes Standard Contractual Clauses and requirements concerning encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, logging, separation and secure deletion.

retention.heading: How long we keep information
blocks: We do not keep every type of information for the same period.
Sogverse account information: kept while the family account is active and then deleted or anonymised, except where a limited record must lawfully be retained.
Programme administration and participation information: kept until Programme delivery, final reporting and reasonable follow-up are complete, then deleted or anonymised.
Roblox research dataset: returned or securely deleted when the relevant processing services end, unless applicable law requires limited retention.
Marketing information: kept until the parent unsubscribes.
Media and media permissions: kept for the permitted reporting or publication purpose and reviewed periodically.
Safeguarding, incident and legal records: may be kept longer where necessary to protect a child, investigate a concern, comply with law, or establish or defend legal claims.
Security records: kept only for the period reasonably needed to protect and investigate the service.
Closing a Sogverse account does not automatically close a separate Roblox account or remove an experience published on Roblox.

rights.heading: Your rights — and your child’s rights
blocks: Depending on the circumstances, the parent and child may ask us to:
Provide access to the personal information held.
Correct inaccurate or incomplete information.
Delete information.
Restrict how information is used.
Provide certain information in a portable format.
Object to processing based on legitimate interests, including identifiable Programme-impact research.
Withdraw an optional consent at any time.
Withdrawing consent does not affect processing that was lawful before withdrawal.
Children may contact us directly about their own information. Parents or legal guardians may also make a request for a child, subject to the child’s own rights, age and maturity.
There is no solely automated decision-making that produces legal or similarly significant effects on participants.
Send requests to support@lynxeducate.com or {supportEmail}. The organisations will coordinate the response and route Roblox-related requests to Roblox where necessary.
Families also have the right to complain to the Commission nationale de l’informatique et des libertés — CNIL.

security.heading: Keeping information safe
blocks: We use measures appropriate to the risks involved, including:
Encryption in transit and at rest.
Hashed passwords.
Role-based access controls.
Access and security logging.
Pseudonymisation where appropriate.
Logical separation of datasets.
Backups and incident-response procedures.
Confidentiality obligations for personnel and contractors.
Restrictions on downloading, copying and reusing participant information.

blocks: We may update this policy if the Programme, its technology or legal requirements change.

parentPin.question: What is the parent PIN, and what if I forget it?
parentPin.answer:
Your parent PIN is a four-digit code you set the first time you use your parent account. It gates the parent side of Sogverse rather than each separate action: you unlock once, and the session locks again the moment you switch to a gamer profile or sign out — so a password saved in the browser is not enough on its own to buy anything or change a child’s account.

If you forget it, tap “Forgot your PIN?” on the PIN screen: we email a reset link to the address on your account and nowhere else, so a child pressing it simply sends you an email. The link lasts 24 hours and works once.

You can also change a PIN you still know from Settings.

sessionReports.question: Will I hear how sessions went?
sessionReports.answer:
Yes. After a session your child’s Game Educator writes a report on it — what the group worked on, how it went, and the moments worth remembering — often with photos.

It appears on that club, camp or event’s page in My SOG, under Sessions, alongside every earlier report and the sessions still to come, and your child sees the same reports in their own My SOG. When the Gedu sends the report, it also arrives by email, addressed to you alone — every family receives their own separate email and no family sees another.

You will also see your own child’s attendance mark for each session on that page; your child does not see attendance, and no family ever sees another child’s.

missedSessions.question: What if we miss a session, or join a club partway through?
missedSessions.answer:
A club stays open for new gamers while it is running, so you can join partway through a term — the club page shows which day and time it meets each week, the term it runs over, and how many seats are left; once your child is enrolled, their own club page names the date of the next session.

Camps and events are different: a camp closes to new sign-ups the day before it starts, because the group starts together, and an event closes once its session has ended.

A club is billed as a full month from the day you sign up, so joining mid-month does not reduce that month’s payment; if a club has not started yet, nothing is charged on the day you sign up and the page tells you the date of your first payment.

If your child misses a single session there is nothing to do — their place is not affected. Their Gedu marks attendance for each session and you will see that mark on the club page. A session missed is not made up or refunded; on a municipality club, repeated unexcused absences may open the place for the next family on the waiting list, which you agree to when you register.

sessionTimes.question: What time do sessions happen in our timezone?
sessionTimes.answer:
In yours. Session times are authored in Finnish time and shown to you converted to your own device’s timezone automatically, everywhere they appear — on a club’s page, on its card, and on your My SOG.

When your timezone differs from the club’s, the time carries a short timezone marker beside it so the conversion is visible; when you are in the same zone as the club, there is nothing to convert and no marker.

Because the conversion is real, a club running on two Finnish weekdays can land on different weekdays for you, and the schedule you see is grouped by your weekdays, not ours. A camp’s start and end dates are plain calendar dates and do not shift.

hero.title: What is <primary>Yty</primary>?
hero.subtitle: Yty is the force that keeps Sogverse in balance. By doing good things — learning new skills, making friends, behaving well, and taking part in the community — gamers earn Yty for themselves and for everyone.

overview.heading: How Yty works
overview.paragraph1: Every gamer starts at zero. From every session attended, every Quest completed, and every act of kindness shown, gamers earn Yty-Points. These points build up across the four Yty-Elements, each reflecting a different part of growing up well.
overview.paragraph2: As gamers collect Yty for themselves, they also raise the total Yty of Sogverse — shaping the story and unlocking new possibilities for the whole community.

elements.heading: The Four Yty-Elements
elements.subheading: Each Yty-Element is one relationship a gamer is growing: with themselves, with others, with society, and with technology

harmony.name: Harmony
harmony.detail: Who am I? Harmony is about accepting yourself as you are — strengths and weaknesses alike. It means learning to take care of your wellbeing, expressing your emotions, making good decisions, and understanding why rules and trust matter.

glow.name: Glow
glow.detail: How can I help others? Glow is about empathy, kindness, and building meaningful relationships. It means respecting differences, giving space to others, communicating well, and being the kind of person who lifts people up.

valor.name: Valor
valor.detail: How can I make a difference? Valor is about finding your place in society and having the courage to contribute to it. It means teamwork, expressing your ideas, using your imagination, and working towards a better future — locally and globally.

wit.name: Wit
wit.detail: How do I handle technology well? Wit is about a healthy, critical relationship with games, media, and the tools around them. It means understanding online behaviour, thinking critically about information, and balancing screen time with the rest of life.

earning.heading: How gamers earn Yty
earning.paragraph1: Yty-Points are earned through participation. Attending weekly club sessions, completing Quests, showing kindness to fellow gamers, joining community events and camps — all of these contribute to a gamer’s Yty.
earning.paragraph2: As points accumulate under specific Achievement Badges, gamers level those badges up — from bronze to silver, gold, platinum, and diamond. Every point also feeds into their overall Yty-Level and the Yty-Element it belongs to.
earning.paragraph3: And it’s not just gamers. Gedus, parents, and the entire community can take part in building the Yty of Sogverse through events and shared activities.

intro.heading: The short version
paragraphs: School of Gaming exists to give children a safe, fun place to learn through gaming. This page lists the main things we hold about your child, and why — in plain language instead of legal jargon, so you can check it for yourself. A gamer account carries an internal Sogverse address rather than a real email, and it exists only inside your own account.

In short: we only collect what we need to run our clubs, camps, and events. We never sell your information or your child’s. Only a parent can create a child’s account, and we never advertise to children. You can ask us to show, correct, or delete your information at any time by emailing {supportEmail}.

whoWeAre.heading: Who we are
paragraphs: Sogverse is run by School of Gaming Galactic Oy ("School of Gaming", "we", "us"), a Finnish company. We’re responsible for looking after the personal information you and your child share with us — in legal terms, we’re the "data controller".
Here are our official details:

Isokatu 56, 90100 Oulu, Finland
Email: {supportEmail}

infoWeCollect.heading: The information we collect
paragraphs: We try to collect as little as possible — only what we genuinely need to run Sogverse. Here’s what that looks like:
bullets: Your name, email address, and (if you add one) phone number — so we can set up your account and keep in touch about your child’s clubs.
Your language and currency preferences — so the site shows up the way you expect.
Your password, which we store only in a scrambled (hashed) form — we can never see it.
Payment details are handled directly in Stripe. We never see or store your full card number.

About your child: their first name, their birth month and year (we don’t ask for the full date — only what we actually need), and optionally their gender — so we can place them in the right group and address them properly. We store your family surname on their account too, because your child is part of your account; Gedus and other gamers never see it. Their account itself uses an internal Sogverse address rather than a real email.

Optionally, your child’s username in the games their clubs use — today that’s Minecraft and Roblox — and the account id that game gives them, so we can recognise them in the game and so they can connect to our Minecraft server during sessions.
Session records our Game Educators write — attendance, session reports, and short notes that help us support your child in the group.
Basic, anonymous information about how the site is used (see "Cookies, analytics and advertising" below).

The campaign tag — source, medium and campaign — carried by the link your visit came from. We store it once, when the account is created, so that we and our partners know which outreach actually reaches families.

childrensPrivacy.heading: Children’s privacy comes first
paragraphs: Most of the people using Sogverse are children, so their safety and privacy is our highest priority.

A child can never create their own account. Only a parent or guardian sets up a child’s account, chooses what to share, and gives permission on their behalf. That’s how we meet our responsibilities under data-protection law when it comes to children.

What we hold about a child is set out above under "The information we collect", and we don’t collect anything about a child beyond what we need to run our clubs, camps, and events. We never show children advertising, and we never sell or share their data for marketing. When your child is signed in as a gamer, nothing about their browsing is sent to an advertising platform, even if marketing is switched on for the device. Live sessions are run by our trained Game Educators (we call them Gedus).
If you ever want to see, change, or delete your child’s information, just email {supportEmail} and we’ll take care of it.

howWeUse.heading: How we use your information
paragraphs: We use the information above only to run Sogverse and give your family a good experience — specifically:
bullets: To create and manage your account and your child’s account.
To place your child in the right club, camp, or event group and connect them with a Game Educator.
To run the live voice and video sessions.
To take payments and send receipts, reminders, and important updates about your clubs.
To answer your questions when you contact us for help.
To keep Sogverse safe, fix problems, and make it better over time.

legalBasis.heading: Why we’re allowed to use it
paragraphs: Data-protection law (the GDPR) asks us to have a clear reason for using your information. Ours are simple:
bullets: To deliver what you signed up for — the clubs and services you’ve bought from us (our contract with you).
Because a parent has given permission on their child’s behalf (consent).
To meet our legal duties, such as keeping accounting records for payments.
For our legitimate interest in keeping the site secure and working well — always balanced against your privacy.
For our legitimate interest in understanding which of our outreach efforts reach families — always balanced against your privacy, and you can ask us to stop at any time.
Your consent, for the analytics and marketing cookies — which you can withdraw at any time from Privacy choices at the bottom of every page.

providers.heading: The companies that help us run Sogverse
paragraphs: Running an online service means relying on a few trusted companies for things like hosting, payments, and email. They only handle your information to do their job for us, under contracts that require them to keep it safe. The main ones are:
bullets: Supabase — securely stores your account, family, and club information.
Stripe — processes payments. Your card details go straight to Stripe; we never see them.
Brevo — sends our emails, such as receipts and reminders.
Daily.co — powers the live voice and video sessions.
Vercel — hosts the website and provides anonymous usage statistics.
Meta (WhatsApp) — used to send some messages and reminders to families who prefer WhatsApp.
Roblox — receives your child’s Roblox account id, so we can confirm the account and show their avatar picture.
Mojang (Microsoft) — receives your child’s Minecraft username, so we can confirm the account.
Meta (Facebook and Instagram ads) — learns, through the Meta Pixel, that you visited and whether you created an account, so we can show our ads there. Only if you allow marketing cookies.
TikTok — learns, through the TikTok Pixel, that you visited and whether you created an account, so we can show our ads on TikTok. Only if you allow marketing cookies.

cookies.heading: Cookies, analytics and advertising
paragraphs: A few cookies are simply how the site works: they keep you signed in, remember that you entered your parent PIN, hold your language and timezone, and store the cookie choice you make. These don’t need your consent — without them there is no site to consent to.

Everything else waits for you. The first time you visit we ask, and nothing beyond those necessary cookies runs until you answer. You can change your mind whenever you like from Privacy choices at the bottom of every page: switching something off takes effect straight away, and it doesn’t change anything we already did while it was on.
There are two things to say yes or no to:
bullets: Analytics — Vercel’s, and only if you choose it. It counts visits, measures how quickly pages load, and receives a few anonymous events about how the site is used: how someone reached their My SOG, when someone changes the language. It can’t see who you are, and we never hand it to advertisers.

Marketing — the Meta Pixel and the TikTok Pixel, and only if you choose them. They learn that you visited School of Gaming and whether you created an account, so Meta and TikTok can show you our ads on their own platforms. Neither pixel loads while your child is signed in as a gamer. If you say yes to marketing and then create an account, we set one short-lived cookie of our own — five minutes, no name, no address, nothing but the word "registration" — whose only job is to tell the pixels on the next page that an account was created. Switching marketing off deletes the cookies the pixels left in your browser, but we can’t delete what Meta and TikTok already hold — you can ask them to, in your own settings there, where Meta calls it "activity off Meta technologies".

voice.heading: Voice and video sessions
paragraphs: Live clubs, camps, and events take place over voice and video, powered by Daily.co. Sessions are run live by our trained Game Educators, and we use it only to deliver the session your child signed up for.

retention.heading: How long we keep your information
paragraphs: We keep your information for as long as you have an account with us. If you close your account, we delete or anonymise your information — except where the law requires us to keep certain records longer, such as Finnish accounting law, which requires payment records to be kept for several years.

storage.heading: Where your information is kept
paragraphs: Some of the companies that help us (listed above) are based outside the European Union, for example in the United States. When your information is sent to them, we make sure it’s protected by the safeguards data-protection law requires — usually the European Commission’s Standard Contractual Clauses.

rights.heading: Your rights — and your child’s
paragraphs: You’re in control of your information. At any time you can ask us to:
bullets: Show you what information we hold about you and your child.
Correct anything that’s wrong.
Delete your information (the "right to be forgotten").
Give you a copy to take elsewhere.
Stop or limit how we use it.

security.heading: Keeping your information safe
paragraphs: We protect your information with industry-standard measures: encrypted connections, passwords stored only in scrambled form, and strict limits on who can access data. No system is ever perfectly secure, but we work hard to keep your family’s information safe.

changes.heading: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: We may update this policy from time to time — for example, if we add a new feature. When we make an important change, we’ll update the date at the top and, where it matters, let you know.

contact.heading: Getting in touch and your right to complain
paragraphs: To use any of the rights above, or if you have a question about your privacy or your child’s information, just email {supportEmail}. There’s no charge, we’ll always reply, and email is the best way to reach us.
If you’re ever unhappy with how we’ve handled your information, you have the right to complain to the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman (Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto) at tietosuoja.fi.

intro.heading: The short version
paragraphs: These are the terms for using Sogverse and signing your child up for our clubs, camps, and events. We’ve written them in plain language, because we want you to actually understand what you’re agreeing to — not wade through legal jargon.

In short: our clubs happen online, run live by our trained Game Educators. You can cancel a monthly club whenever you like, and every club carries a 30-day money-back guarantee — if it isn’t right for your child, tell us within 30 days of their first session and we refund you in full. If you ever have a question, email {supportEmail} and a real person will help.

service.heading: How our clubs work
paragraphs: Almost everything we do happens online — your child joins their club, camp, or event from home, through our website. If a particular product works differently (for example, an in-person event), we’ll always say so clearly on that product’s page before you buy.

games.heading: The games your child plays
paragraphs: Our clubs are built around video games made by other companies, such as Minecraft. We follow Finland’s official age-rating guidance.

In practice this means a child may play a game rated for up to three years above their own age, as long as a parent is present and comfortable with it — but never a game rated 18+. When you sign your child up, you’re confirming you’re happy with the age ratings of the games involved.

online.heading: Staying safe online
paragraphs: The tools we use for live sessions have their own minimum-age rules, set by the companies that make them and by local law. To keep things safe and above board, children under 13 take part using their parent’s account. Sessions are run live by our trained Game Educators (we call them Gedus).

pricing.heading: Prices and payment
paragraphs: All prices are shown in euros and include VAT. We may change our prices from time to time, but a change will never affect a club you’re already paying for without us telling you first.

clubsCancellation.heading: Cancelling a monthly club
paragraphs: Our clubs run as a monthly subscription, and you’re free to cancel whenever you like — there’s no fixed commitment. You can do it yourself from your account, and your child keeps their place until the end of the month you’ve already paid for.

We also want you to be able to try us with confidence, so every club comes with a 30-day money-back guarantee. If it turns out not to be right for your child, email {supportEmail} within 30 days of their first session and we’ll refund everything you have paid towards that club. There’s no form to fill in and no reason to give.

campsCancellation.heading: Cancelling a camp
paragraphs: Camps are booked and paid for as a one-off, so the cancellation terms are a little different. If you need to cancel a camp:
bullets: 14 days or more before the camp starts: you get a full refund.
Between 7 and 14 days before: we refund you minus a €50 administration fee.
Less than 7 days before: we’re unable to refund the payment, because the place has been held and prepared for your child — unless it’s a medical emergency or something genuinely outside your control.
If your child can’t attend because of illness, we’ll refund you when you send us a doctor’s certificate at {supportEmail}.

conduct.heading: Behaviour and removing a child from a club
paragraphs: We want every child to feel safe and welcome, so we don’t tolerate bullying or behaviour that spoils things for others. When a problem comes up, we always start by supporting the child and helping them put it right — our full approach is set out in our <linkDiscipline>Anti-Bullying and Discipline policy</linkDiscipline>.
Only after those supportive steps, and in the case of ongoing toxic or disruptive behaviour or bullying, may we end a child’s participation. We’ll always talk it through with you first.

privacy.heading: Your family’s privacy
paragraphs: We handle your family’s information in line with Finnish and EU data-protection law, and we hold as little of your child’s as we can: a gamer account is created by you, carries an internal Sogverse address rather than your child’s own email, and is never used to advertise to them. Our <linkPrivacy>Privacy Policy</linkPrivacy> explains exactly what we collect and why.

contact.heading: Getting in touch

intro.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Every child should feel safe, respected, and welcome in our clubs. Bullying and unkindness have no place here — and the Sogverse platform has no direct-message feature: conversation happens in shared group spaces, and chat during a call goes to the whole room and is never stored.

When something goes wrong, we don’t just punish — we help. We use a calm, step-by-step approach that focuses on helping a child understand what happened, make it right, and do better next time. We only move to a firmer step if the behaviour keeps happening, and we keep you informed the whole way through.

commitment.heading: Children first. Always.
paragraphs: Our clubs are a place to learn, make friends, and have fun — and that only works if everyone feels safe. We’re committed to a community free of bullying, harassment, and cruelty, where every child is treated with respect by our Game Educators and by each other.

approach.heading: How we handle problems
paragraphs: When a child behaves in a way that hurts or disrupts others, our Game Educators (we call them Gedus) respond in a way that’s calm, kind, and right for the child’s age. The goal is always to help the child understand the effect of what they did and to put it right — not simply to punish.

We deal with most situations gently, with a quiet word. If the behaviour continues, we take firmer steps, one at a time. The steps below are the ladder we follow, and you’ll always be kept in the loop as we go.

step1.heading: Step 1 — A reminder and putting things right
paragraphs: The Gedu talks with your child about what happened and how it affected others, and helps them find a better way to handle it. It’s gentle and matter-of-fact — for example: "Remember not to take things from someone else’s chest without asking. You could ask them if they’d like to trade instead."

step2.heading: Step 2 — A quiet word
paragraphs: If it happens again, the Gedu has a one-on-one chat with your child to think through what they did and how it affects others. We’ll also let you know at home that we’ve talked with your child about their behaviour in the club.

step3.heading: Step 3 — Stepping in during the session
paragraphs: If the disruptive behaviour carries on, the Gedu steps in to stop it during the session — for example by muting your child for a moment or limiting what they can do in the game. The Gedu speaks with your child privately, and we message you at home.

step4.heading: Step 4 — A time-out from a session
paragraphs: If things still don’t settle, the Gedu may ask your child to sit out the rest of that session. If a longer break is needed, we’ll tell you in advance. The Gedu talks it through privately with your child, we message you at home, and our office ({supportEmail}) joins the conversation.

step5.heading: Step 5 — Time away from the community
paragraphs: If the behaviour continues despite everything above, a child may be removed from the School of Gaming community for a while — that means their clubs, and Sogverse itself, including our game servers. Our office gets in touch with you to explain the decision, and we talk it through with your child too.

step6.heading: Step 6 — A fresh start later
paragraphs: Time away isn’t necessarily the end. Your child can come back when you and they both feel ready for it. If they return and the behaviour hasn’t changed, we’ll step them out of the activity for good rather than starting the ladder over — but our hope, always, is a fresh start that works.

partnership.heading: We’re in this together
paragraphs: You know your child best, and we get the best results when we work together. If you have any worries about how your child is getting on — or if you think they’re being treated unkindly by someone else — please tell us. Sharing the same expectations at home and in the club makes a real difference.

contact.heading: Getting in touch
paragraphs: If you have any questions about this policy, or you’d like to talk about something that’s happened, email our office at {supportEmail}. There’s a real person at the other end, and we’re here to help.
